Patterns

Six patterns at a glance

The candle bodies show open-to-close movement; the thin lines show each period’s high and low. These simplified drawings illustrate the shapes, not a trading recommendation.

Doji · indecision

The opening and closing prices are nearly the same, leaving a tiny body. A doji can signal a pause or uncertainty; by itself, it does not confirm a reversal.

Bullish engulfing · possible reversal

A bullish candle’s body fully covers the previous bearish body. Traders often study it after a decline as a possible shift in momentum; context and follow-through matter.

Hammer · possible bullish reversal

A small body sits near the high, with a much longer lower wick. After a decline it may suggest buyers pushed prices back up; confirmation is important.

Bearish engulfing · possible reversal

A bearish candle’s body fully covers the previous bullish body. After an advance it may suggest momentum is changing, but the pattern alone cannot predict what follows.

Morning star · three-candle turn

A long bearish candle is followed by a small-bodied pause and then a strong bullish candle. It is studied as a possible shift after a decline, not a guarantee.

Evening star · three-candle turn

The opposite sequence—a long bullish candle, small pause, and strong bearish candle—is studied as a possible shift after an advance. Context and confirmation matter.

A candlestick summarizes price movement over a set period. Its body shows the opening and closing prices, while its wicks mark the high and low. Candlestick patterns are recognizable arrangements of one or more candles—such as a doji, engulfing pattern, or morning star—that traders study for clues about momentum, indecision, or a possible reversal. They are signals to investigate, not guarantees of what the market will do next.

This project turns those chart-reading rules into a repeatable research workflow. It scans historical stock prices for configurable patterns across symbols, compares what happened over the following 1–12 trading sessions, and presents date-, symbol-, and industry-filtered reports with charts. The goal is to explore and compare how patterns behaved across historical data at scale, rather than manually inspect charts one by one; past results do not predict future returns.
